vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the chair with his shoulders drawn inward, a posture that seems almost permanent now. At forty-six, he carries himself like someone much older-the kind of weariness that comes not from a single bad night but from years of accumulated dread. He was a firefighter for eighteen years before taking a leave of absence, a career that had always suited him. He was good at rushing toward danger, at staying calm when others panicked. But that was before.

Four years ago, Marcus took a sabbatical to work with an international relief organization in a region torn apart by conflict. His ex-wife thought it was noble; his colleagues thought he was crazy. Marcus himself isn't entirely sure what drove him there. He remembers wanting to feel useful in a way that fighting fires-however important-no longer satisfied. He was restless, searching for something he couldn't name.

The first month was difficult but manageable. Marcus worked in a makeshift clinic, helping to distribute medical supplies and assist with basic triage. He saw things that disturbed him-malnourished children, untreated wounds, the blank stares of people who had lost everything. But he could compartmentalize it, the way he'd learned to do with fire scenes. Then came the day that changed everything.

The clinic was hit during a sudden escalation of violence. Marcus was in the back room when the explosion occurred. He doesn't remember much about the immediate aftermath-a kind of merciful blank space. What he does remember is crawling out from under rubble, his ears ringing, and finding one of the local nurses, a woman named Amara who had become his friend, pinned under a collapsed beam. He remembers the weight of her, the warmth of her blood on his hands, the way her eyes found his as she struggled to breathe. He remembers that she died while he was trying to free her.

He was evacuated the next day. The organization called it a medical evacuation, though physically he was largely unharmed.

Since returning home, Marcus exists in a strange fog. He lives alone in the same house where he and his ex-wife raised their two adult children, though they barely speak now. He told them he was fine, that he just needed time, and they've respected that distance-or perhaps they've simply accepted his withdrawal as permanent.

The hypervigilance is constant. Every unexpected sound makes his body tense; he finds himself cataloging exits wherever he goes. He's stopped going to the grocery store at busy times. The smell of smoke, which once meant something manageable and professional, now sends him into a spiral of panic. He'll sit in his car in the driveway for twenty minutes before he can bring himself to go inside, convinced something terrible is about to happen.

Sleep is fragmented and unreliable. When he does sleep, he's back in the clinic-sometimes he's still trying to save Amara, sometimes he's buried under the rubble himself. He wakes gasping, his heart hammering against his ribs.

He hasn't returned to the fire department. He can't imagine suiting up, climbing into a truck, trusting his body to respond the way it once did. His captain has stopped calling. Marcus tells himself this is fine, that maybe this chapter of his life is simply over. But mostly he feels untethered, like a man who volunteered to be useful and instead discovered something broken inside himself that usefulness can no longer reach.
